title: a Cassavettes movie for me? Asking for Recs and Discussion on A Woman Under the Influence.

commenti.body: I enjoyed “Killing of a Chinese Bookie” and “Gloria”, but maybe Cassavettes isn’t for you right now.   “Lost in America” is a funny, understated movie by Albert Brooks that I just rewatched.

I think A Woman Under the Influence is an incredibly hopeful, uplifting movie. Yes, it does show how difficult it is to not just love, but to be in a relationship with someone. But it also shows how important these things are to people, that no matter how hard it gets, they won’t quit. That’s an immensely positive way of looking at the world. Most of the time I worry about whether or not other people care about these things as much as I do, and with a movie like this, Cassavetes is saying yeah they care about this stuff to the point where it’s the most important thing in their lives. 

All I’m saying with this is that I think if you shift the way you’re looking at his movies, you’ll find a lot the joy that’s in them. Hard joy, but joy nonetheless. 

Try Minnie and Moskowitz next. It’s a little easier to find the positivity in that one.

A Woman Under the Influence is indeed exhausting. It's not one I watch much, and he's my favorite director.

I always recommend to start with Minnie and Moskowitz. It's his most comedic film, probably has the best flow of any of his movies.

Shadows and Husbands (if you're a dude) are good follow ups.

A Killing of a Chinese Bookie is wonderful. The movie of his I watch the most. But it can be dense.

Mikey and Nicky is technically an Elaine May film, but it plays like a Cassavetes film to the point where Cassavetes scholar Ray Carney argues that he took over directing duties for the most part from her. It's also much more approachable than Woman Under the Influence.
If you're a dude??? 😭😭😭
True. it's great to see artists portraying these things and I appreciate it very much. But I think I need a hug lol

I mean I don't know your pronouns, lol. I'm not stalking your profile.

But Husbands is a very man based film, whereas Woman Under the Influence reflects 70's female domestic struggles as a counterpoint.

Btw, Cassavetes' absolute masterpiece is Faces. So if you just want to speedrun his works, you can just watch that.

Here's a good interview with Cassavetes to better understand his objective:

https://youtu.be/ePptcNqXRJA?si=qRTM1Kg13WTWFkLh
I'm a dude and Husbands was too manly for me.

If you’re looking for any conventional kind of “popcorn movie” kind of enjoyment from Cassavetes you’ve definitely come to the wrong place. In that “A Constant Forge” documentary I remember him saying something to the effect that he enjoyed seeing people walk out of screenings of his films because what he ultimately wants is for people’s lives to be less difficult, less painful in comparison to (the experience of watching) his movies. Personally of his work what I like best are Faces, …Chinese Bookie, and Opening Night. As for WUTI, I’ve tried about 3 times to watch it but I always ditch it midway, it’s just the absolute worst imo.

It's so funny bc everyone was recommended AWUTI as an intro to cassavettes but now ppl r saying it's his most difficult and exhausting watch lol. That's such a crazy quote too. Once I recover from watching this I'll have to give him another shot and maybe his empathy will connect more.
I feel like Cassavetes gives you the hug by acknowledging these things. It’s like him saying you’re not alone in this stuff.
In my opinion, Husbands, Faces, and Love Streams are harder watches than A Woman Under the Influence. It may sound weird, but Mabel and Nick are probably his most secure in their love couple haha.

AWUTI is indeed exhausting. I liked it but didn't love it. I felt a little disconnected from it. I haven't watched anything from Cass in years but I remember loving Chinese Bookie, in fact it's one of my favorite films of all time. I would go with that or Faces; Faces was the first Cass film I saw and I loved it, had that kinetic first-timer filmmaker energy to it, though it wasn't his first. 

I don't know, you just have to watch a few more to find out.

My impression of Cassavettes is this; he makes memories, not movies. I got the blu-ray collection of his directed films (only made through a German press for whatever reason) and every few years - hell, decade, when I rewatch them I am struck with how much of each film I remember. 

You're right, there's no takeaway. No "hope", but you never forget them. I think that is a very admirable quality in a film. You are compelled even though it's not enjoyable.

If you want something a little weird and random I highly recommend Cassavettes as an actor - to me this is where he becomes truly understandable. He is an actor first and all his direction is in service to the art of acting. Opening Night is the perfect example.

But I fell in love with this little Shakespeare adaptation he did in 1982. Tempest. [This is my longer argument for it](https://medium.com/@jandrist/tempest-1982-the-greatest-movie-of-all-time-5c2e7dab7104)
I loved the opening scenes of Gloria, those first 15-ish minutes. The rest is fine, too, but the beginning is maybe the best stuff he ever made IMO

I lived in Budapest in the mid-90s and there was a small theatre that only played Cassavetes films (acting and directing) and I fell in love with his work over the course of a year.

A Woman Under the Influence is one of my faves from him because so much of Gena Rowland's Mabel and her story  reminds me of the women in my family as I was growing up. Obviously it's a tough watch when I revisit the film but it's also cathartic in a way. 

Not all films need to be escapist fantasies that finish with no loose ends and tidy bows on top. I totally understand why people go that route but it's also not for everyone.
He's a great villain in DePalma's The Fury.

I’m surprised no one had mentioned Love Streams yet. It’s meandering, but not as punishing as some of his others. In my opinion, it’s more redemptive in its depiction of familial bonds.

What I love about A Woman Under the Influence is what seems to have exasperated you. I remember feeling worn out afterward, but I didn’t stop thinking about it for about three weeks. I didn’t know how to feel about what I’d seen. And when I watched it again a few years later, it really clicked for me. Sometimes movies are great because they’re complicated and overwhelming. And I know people who have lived through situations like the one depicted, and while it may not be specific or “accurate,” it feels very true to their experiences.

It could also be that Cassavetes is not your jam, and that’s okay, too.  But he’s worth exploring further.

I don't need my movies to be escapist fantasies I just think that if I was in those situations irl I would stop fucking screaming lol. Maybe I'm just not at s point in my life where I can I engage with this film bc it low-key made me sick but maybe if I'm in a better more mature mental state I could get more from it idk.

Slightly related, if you haven't yet seen I'm Thinking of Ending Things then I would recommend it while AWUTI is still in your head as their are some references to it.

I had a similar experience to you. I first watched this movie when I was in my early twenties and I found it unbearable. Some film buff friends showed it to me, and didn’t get why I made such a big deal.

I watched it again when I was 40, and this time I was introducing it to my wife. We had gone through so much in the previous decade with my step-son’s wild high school years, our  younger kid’s medical issues, the experience of being out of work for long periods, etc. The movie somehow seemed very charming this time. Very real and very charming. Gena Rowlands gives one of the all-time performances. The scene where Peter Falk takes the kids to the beach is so funny. 

I guess what I want to say is, to the younger people out there, maybe try the movie again in middle age and see if it hits different.
